Empirical Research Plan – “Why Do Developing Countries Tax the Way They Do?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  

Strategy chosen: Cross-country Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) design.  

Rationale  
• The research question is structural – we want the causal effect of one deep friction (the size of the cash/informal economy that impedes third–party reporting) on the observed tax mix.  
• With only 5–6 annual observations per country (1996-2001) and no obvious common shock that differentially hits treated and control countries, DID or event studies have little power.  
• The informal sector share is endogenous: governments with weak capacity may both tolerate informality and adopt particular tax structures. We therefore need instruments that shift informality for reasons orthogonal to contemporaneous tax-policy choices.  
• A cross-sectional 2SLS using long-run, predetermined determinants of financial depth and cash intensity (which in turn drive informality) is the most credible approach with these data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable (endogenous regressor)  
Informality_it  = Informal economy (% of GDP) for country i (Schneider, 2002; 1999 observation used for all years).  
It is continuous; for exposition we will sometimes speak of “high-informality” countries (top quintile) versus the rest.

Instrument set Z_i  (all measured long before 1996)  
1. LegalOrigin_i – dummies for British, French, Socialist/Communist, German/Scandinavian (La Porta et al.).  
2. HistoricalRuggedness_i × PopulationDensity1960_i – rugged, densely populated terrain historically hampers bank branch expansion and electronic infrastructure.  
3. TelephoneLines1960_i / Pop – an early, plausibly exogenous proxy for the ease of electronic/third-party reporting.  

Control (counterfactual) group  
Countries with similar income levels and regions but low predicted informality given the instruments serve as the counterfactual.

Timing  
Cross-section of countries averaged over 1996-2001. No single event date is required.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Instrument relevance – Legal origin, historical ruggedness × density, and 1960 telephone penetration are strongly correlated with 1999 informal-economy size because they shaped long-run financial and information-reporting capacity.  
Plausibility: Documented in the finance-and-growth and geography literatures.

A2. Exclusion – Conditional on 1996 GDP per capita, region fixed effects, and other controls, the instruments affect today’s tax composition only through their impact on informality/financial depth.  
Plausibility: Tax structure evolved mainly in the 1970s-1990s; 1960 communications stock and colonial legal origin influence current institutions primarily via enforcement capacity, not explicit tax-policy mandates.

A3. Monotonicity – Countries that would have a larger informal sector under one instrument value (e.g. French legal origin) would not instead become more formal if we moved them to another instrument value (e.g. British).  
Plausibility: Direction of influence is well-established.

A4. No perfect multicollinearity or weak instruments – First-stage F > 10.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  

T1. Omitted geographic or colonial factors that influence both instruments and modern tax preferences directly (e.g. French-origin countries also choosing VAT earlier).  
Mitigation: Include colonial-empire fixed effects, year-since-independence, and current trade-openness controls; perform over-identification (Hansen J) tests.

T2. Measurement error in informal-sector estimates (derived from the currency-demand approach).  
Mitigation: (i) Use multiple sources (e.g. Elgin & Öztunali 2014) in robustness; (ii) 2SLS already attenuates classical measurement error; (iii) re-run with informality quintile dummies.

T3. Weak instruments / weak first stage.  
Mitigation: Combine three historically strong predictors; report first-stage F-statistics, use LIML/Anderson-Rubin confidence sets; collapse to 2-way legal-origin instrument as placebo.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# -------------  SET-UP  -------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast 2SLS
library(modelsummary) # neat tables
# If weak-IV concern:
library(ivreg)       # provides LIML
# -------------  DATA  -------------
df <- read_csv("macro_fiscal_9699.csv")  # each row country-year 1996-2001
informal <- read_csv("informal_share_1999.csv") # one obs per country
df <- df %>% 
  left_join(informal, by = "iso3c") %>% 
  group_by(iso3c) %>% 
  summarise(across(c(total_revgdp,
                     pers_inc_tax_share,
                     corp_tax_share,
                     trade_tax_share,
                     seignorage_share,
                     inflation,
                     gdp_pc,
                     informal_share), mean, na.rm = TRUE),
            region = first(region),
            legal_origin = first(legal_origin),
            rugged = first(rugged),
            popdens1960 = first(popdens1960),
            tel60 = first(tel60))

# -------------  INSTRUMENTS -------------
df <- df %>%
  mutate(rugged_dens = rugged * popdens1960)

# -------------  MAIN SPECIFICATION -------------
# Equation: TaxComponent_i = α + β * Informal_i (endogenous) + γX + ε
iv_formula <- corp_tax_share ~ informal_share + log(gdp_pc) + inflation + region | 
                             log(gdp_pc) + inflation + region +
                             legal_origin + rugged_dens + tel60

est1 <- feols(iv_formula, data = df, se = "hetero")
summary(est1, stage = 1:2)

# -------------  ROBUSTNESS: ALTERNATIVE DEP VAR -------------
est2 <- feols(trade_tax_share ~ informal_share + log(gdp_pc) + region |
                                 log(gdp_pc) + region + legal_origin +
                                 rugged_dens + tel60,
              data = df, se = "hetero")

# -------------  WEAK-IV ROBUST STANDARD ERRORS -------------
est1_liml <- ivreg(iv_formula, data = df)
summary(est1_liml, diagnostics = TRUE)

# -------------  OVERID TEST -------------
modelsummary(list(est1, est2),
             gof_omit = "Adj|Within",
             stars = TRUE)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS (PRIORS)  

Theory predicts that difficulty auditing households (large informality) pushes governments to:  
• Shift away from personal income taxes and broad VATs toward narrow-base taxes that can be collected at chokepoints (corporate, trade, and seignorage).  

Magnitudes (ball-park):  
• A 10-percentage-point (pp) higher informal share →  
    – Total tax/GDP −2 pp  
    – Personal income-tax share −1.5 pp  
    – Corporate-tax share +0.8 pp  
    – Trade-tax share +0.7 pp  
    – Inflation (CPI) +3 pp (reflecting reliance on seignorage)  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV design)  

C1. Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) ………………… 1  
C2. Exclusion restriction credible after controls ……………… 0.5  
C3. Monotonicity (direction of effect uniform) ………………… 1  
C4. Over-identification passes Hansen J (p > 0.10) ………… 0.5  
C5. Robust to alternative instrument sets & samples ………… 0.5  

Total score = 3.5 / 5 – credible but not bullet-proof; results must be interpreted with caution and subjected to extensive sensitivity analysis.
